## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kumbhilajātaka* (Ja 224; also spelled *Kumbhīlajātaka*) is a canonical birth-story preserved in the *Jātaka* collection of the Pali Sutta Piṭaka [Fausböll 1879]. According to the narrative framework, the Buddha delivered the story while residing at the Bamboo Grove (Veḷuvana) in Rājagaha concerning his rival Devadatta [Fausböll 1879].

The verses of the text center on an encounter involving a monkey chief (*vānarinda*) and a crocodile (*kumbhīla*), encapsulating an ethical lesson on overcoming enemies through moral qualities [Fausböll 1879]. The verses state that anyone endowed with four virtues—truth (*sacca*), righteousness (*dhamma*), courage or firmness (*dhiti*), and relinquishment (*cāgo*)—overcomes an adversary (*diṭṭhaṁ so ativattati*), whereas one lacking these noble qualities fails to triumph [Fausböll 1879].

 Algorithmic analysis by DharmaNexus records two matches of Pali-internal text reuse with the second volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (matching up to 348 characters, segments §0.4–2.4 aligning with §1306–1310 at a similarity of 0.95), reflecting the commentary's integration of the canonical verses [DharmaNexus].
